subtopic: STATEMENT ON AVAILABILITY OF NEW COIN SETS

speakeroldname: Hon. Waller L. Gordon (Minisler of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: STATEMENT ON AVAILABILITY OF NEW COIN SETS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a few days ago I stated that I hoped shortly to be in a position to inform the House concerning the present situation of the Mint with regard to the production of mint sets of uncirculated coins, and to advise the public as to when the Mint will be ready once again to accept orders from people whose requirements have not yet been met. I am now in a position to report on these questions.
It will be remembered that at the beginning of this year the Mint was confronted with an enormous wave of orders for these coins, estimated at some 6 million sets. To handle this unprecedented situation it was decided at that time that the Mint would accept all orders received on the first day, which happened to be January 2, and would ship the coins thereafter as and when the sets could be produced. These orders involved some 2 million sets. The remaining orders, covering another 4 million sets, had to be returned to the senders. However, I explained at the time that as and when the facilities of the Mint could be expanded later in the year, it would be able to give its attention to these unsatisfied needs.
To fill the orders for the 2 million sets in question the Mint took on additional staff, and for most of the time since January has been operating three shifts a day and six days a week. I think the employees of the Mint are to be warmly commended for the way they have pitched in to help cope with this unusual situation.

subtopic: STATEMENT ON AVAILABILITY OF NEW COIN SETS
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: STATEMENT ON AVAILABILITY OF NEW COIN SETS
speechtext:
As a result of these efforts, it is now estimated that up to yesterday 1,-
100,000	sets have been shipped out to collectors. It is expected that the balance of these 2 million sets will be produced and shipped out before the end of July. I should mention that not quite all the additional requests which the Mint accepted last January 2
have been acknowledged as yet, but these requests will also be acknowledged, and the coin sets shipped to the senders, before the end of July.
[DOT] (2:40 p.m.)
While this accelerated production of Mint sets has been going on the Mint has also been busy acquiring additional accommodation and equipment for its numismatic section. Additional space has been obtained in the Government Printing Bureau in Hull, and this space is now being made suitable and secure. The additional coin presses and other equipment ordered some time ago are expected to be delivered in another week or two and will be installed shortly. This will have the effect of doubling the existing facilities for the production of these coin sets. Additional packaging and distribution facilities have also been set up. In other words, the new machines should be ready to roll very soon. Consequently, by the end of July, when we expect that all of the initial 2 million sets will have been shipped out, the Mint can begin to produce sets to meet the requirements of those whose orders had to be returned earlier in the year, and of any others who are entitled to purchase sets.
I therefore wish to advise the House that beginning today the Mint will resume accepting orders for 1965 sets of uncirculated coins from all who want them and whose requirements are not already met, or are not in the process of being met, by the arrangements I have just described. I repeat the undertaking I gave publicly at the beginning of the year, that the production of these 1965 coin sets will be continued until all legitimate orders have been filled, even if it takes the remainder of 1965 and part of 1966 to finish the job. Requests will be filled, of course, in the order in which they are received. However, in view of the large numbers involved, I must emphasize that it may well be some months after July before all orders can be filled.
The conditions of the sale are unchanged. That is, orders will be accepted for one, three or five sets per person, with a maximum of five sets per person, at a price of $4 per set. Each order for a set or sets should be accompanied by a remittance and be in the name of a single individual. Such orders

April 29, 1965
Royal Canadian Mint
must be regarded as final, so that subsequent cancellations cannot be accepted. Persons whose earlier applications have been met, or have been accepted by the Mint, should not apply for additional sets. Applicants who have not yet received an acknowledgement from the Mint but whose applications have not been returned, should assume that their requests have been accepted by the Mint. Their sets will be delivered before the end of July.
I should also mention that some current shipments from the Mint are being returned with requests that they be remailed to other addresses. I have agreed that the Mint will charge $1 to cover the additional labour and other costs incurred by the Mint in providing this service.
One last word, Mr. Speaker, concerning speculation in Mint sets. In view of the assurance I gave to the public earlier this year, and which I now repeat, that the Mint will be able to provide everyone with his or her full entitlement, there should be no need for ordinary collectors to pay high speculative prices for these coin sets. Everyone will be able to obtain their requirements of up to five sets at the issue price of $4 per set.

Mr. Speaker, the House will recall that yesterday at 17.00 hours I was referring to the role of the provinces in relation to Canadian economic conditions. I had pointed out that natural resources are controlled by the provinces and therefore Federal policies perhaps had very little effect on economic growth. I had also mentioned that the amount of goods which Canadians returning from visiting other countries are allowed to bring back to Canada had, accord-

I was encouraged a bit by an expression used by the Minister of Finance on television the other evening when he was being interviewed by Michael Barkway, Scott Gordon and Norman DePoe of the C.B.C. I thought I sensed, during this interview, that perhaps the Minister was toying in the back of his mind with the idea of making the Bank of Canada a much more effective institution for the public good. I sincerely hope he will take this to heart and do something about it. This is the greatest opportunity for the Government to move in this direction. In British Columbia, as in the Province of Alberta we have followed the simple concept that salaries and wages paid out for the production of goods are not enough to buy back the goods so produced, and therefore we have to have what we call an industrial climate or financial vacuum to attract outside capital into the Province so the total purchasing power of the people of British Columbia can buy back the total production of that Province.
In this connection I might say it is predicted that in Prince George, which is my home town, in the next two years no less than $400 million will be spent in capital expansion. Actually it is a city of about 25,000 or 30,000 today. I can recall, not too long ago, when there were only a few thousand people there. This $400 million, Mr. Speaker, is a lot of capital expansion. It is based on the concept that you must have an industrial climate or financial vacuum to attract capital. We used the Pacific Great Eastern Railway, the Toll Authority and the Hydro Authority to bring about this financial vacuum.
Just briefly, Mr. Speaker, I should like to refer to a couple of other strange things which I feel are happening in the country. First of all I should like to mention that many times we are asked to donate to a cancer fund. We are asked to give and give for research into cancer. At the same time we find ourselves paying out money to advertise the very thing we have found is contributing to cancer, that is cigarettes. It does seem to me we are like the individual who has a leaky boat, and while he is floating on the lake he decides he is going to fix it so he bores a hole in the bottom of the boat to let the water out. I do not see how we can expect to get people seriously interested in the cancer proposition if we are going to allow the advertising which tobacco companies are conducting to continue to get our young people into the habit of smoking cigarettes, which we know contribute not only to lung cancer but to other disabilities of the individual.
The Budget-Mr. Leboe
Now, we hear many tear-jerking stories about people who suffer from poverty in other countries. What do we do? We make grandiose speeches about what we should be doing to help these people. Every day I go by a brewery in this city. I know I am going by it because I can smell it. It smells just like a pig sty with all those rotting husks of grain. We are turning hundreds of thousands of tons of grain into alcohol so it may be consumed, and we are advertising this so that it may be consumed, thus making our No. 1 killer an even greater killer on the highways of our country.
I do not know why we do not settle down and give some thought to where we are going. We talk about speed artists. I want to tell you that statistics show that a man who has had two drinks is a potentially greater killer than a man who is completely drunk. If we are going to spend our time raising grain to make liquor to kill people on the highways, then I think we ought to give some consideration to what Mr. Gaglardi has said on a number of occasions at the safety council meetings in this country.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have listened very carefully to the budget speech of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) three days ago. The first impression of the ordinary listener in the galleries was that everything is fine in Canada, that there is nothing wrong.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I hear someone saying "hear, hear" and applauding. Let him go and applaud such a statement in his own riding; I am afraid he will come back faster than he went, because the unemployed, the farmers and even his own electors are not convinced that everything is fine.
My first reaction was one of bewilderment in the face of such a piece of bluff. They bragged that they had done everything. The government took credit for getting the country out of the doldrums and taking it to the zenith of economic development.
The first reaction in the face of such bragging is bewilderment. But after reflection and checking, the budget speech can be described as a great hoax through biased statistics and garbled figures.
Mr. Speaker, I will refer to the figures supplied by the Minister of Finance as well as to the D.B.S. statistics, and we will be able to see whether the Minister of Finance was right in claiming that everything is fine in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, here is what can be read on page 2 of the French version of the release issued by the Minister of Finance concerning his budget speech:
When this government first came into office, we stated a number of economic objectives. Our first goaf was a high level of employment for Canadians and the reduction of unemployment. The second was a high and sustainable level of economic growth. Thirdly, we wanted a better regional balance in both employment and growth.
So, the first objective that the government stated when it came into office was a high level of employment and a reduction of unemployment.
Now, Mr. Speaker, let us take a look at things according to statistics. I have here a copy of the Statistical Review of Canada, catalogue No. 11-003F, for the month of April 1965. The minister quoted certain figures on unemployment, but his figures do not tally with the actual figures. In fact, the Statistical

Review of Canada publishes completely different figures, and there is even confusion or contradiction in the statistics published in the Statistical Review of Canada.
For instance, we note that in order to explain a decrease of unemployment, the Statistical Review of Canada must bring out a decrease in the civilian labour force in Canada, which is completely contrary to facts, because the Canadian population has increased in every age group. Ten months ago, we were told that the gainfully employed population in Canada numbered 6,901,000, although it was only 6,844,000 in February 1965.
In July 1964, it was said to be 7,232,000 although it was only 6,844,000 in January 1965, which means that the Statistical Review of Canada even cuts down on the Canadian civil labour force and this, of course, is impossible. As a matter of fact, it even reduces the number of people employed in Canada. While there were 6,608,000 employed persons in May 1964, their number was said to be 6,446,000, a drop of 150,000, in February 1965.
Even the number of unemployed is being reduced, which would mean, according to the figures quoted by the minister, that everything is going down in Canada: the population, the number of workers and the number of unemployed persons.
According to the Statistical Review of Canada, there were 408,000 unemployed in the country. Those are official figures. On the other hand, according to the unemployment insurance commission, 547,800 persons were receiving unemployment insurance benefits, or 140,000 more than the number of unemployed quoted in the Statistical Review of Canada.
As I said, we are left with the impression that statistics are deceitfully cut down because, according to the Statistical Review of Canada, there would be 408,000 unemployed in the country even though 547,800 persons are receiving unemployment insurance benefits.
This last figure represents only the number of persons receiving unemployment insurance benefits and does not include those thousands in Quebec receiving social assistance and welfare allowances.

Second objective set by the present government: a high and sustainable rate of economic growth. Mr. Speaker, in reviewing the economic growth of the country from 1961 to 1964, we find that the rate of economic growth has not been high and sustained as claimed by the minister.
In 1961, our gross national product, at the market price, was $38.6 billion; at the end of 1964, it was $46,736 million. The minister is basing himself on those figures to tell us that we have had a 6 per cent and an 8.5 per cent increase. There has been an increase of $8,136 million during those three years, according to the Minister's figures. And there again, Mr. Speaker, the figures given and the actual ones are entirely different, because prices have increased, and this is why the production volume has increased according to the figures quoted.
If a quart of milk which cost 24 cents in 1961 now costs 26 cents, it is obvious that production of a quart of milk is now worth 26 cents. But in 1961, the same quart of milk represented a production of 24 cents. The sale price and not production has been increased. It is merely a price increase.

But that is not all, Mr. Speaker. There was an increase of $5,176 million in constant dollars, but at the same time, in addition to the differences between the price of goods, other amounts were included in this $5,176 million increase. For instance, direct taxes have increased: federal, provincial and municipal taxes. In 1961, they reached $2,564 million; in 1964, $3,424 million, or an increase of $860 million which must be deducted from the $5,176 million increase.
There were also the direct taxes on corporations that must be included in this increase in the gross national product, that is an increase of $208 million in 1964 as compared to 1961.
Indirect taxes must also be included in the gross national product in constant dollars. There was an increase of $1,544 million in 1964 as compared to 1961; that adds up to a total of $2,812 million which must be deducted from the $5,176 million increase in the economic growth of this country.
This gives an actual increase in three years of $2,364 million and not $8,136 million as the Minister of Finance would lead Canadian citizens to believe.
Two billion three hundred and sixty four million dollars in three years, that means an average of 6.5 per cent or an actual average of about 2.2 per cent per year. I do not anticipate difficulties in financing outside Canada the moderate amounts really required for this purpose, but this dependence on foreign savings should not be permitted to persist indefinitely.
And he added:
The major source of capital, the United States, is having to restrict its investments abroad.

Mr. Speaker, the minister also mentioned federal-provincial relations in his budget speech? I should like to quote a sentence from the budget speech, as reported on page 431 of Hansard for April 26, 1965:
The federal government's responsibility in the field of fiscal policy, monetary policy and trade policy is primary and indisputable. And this is as it should be..
But how did the government discharged its responsibility in the field of fiscal policy? It encroached upon the rights of the provinces in the field of direct taxation. The monetary policy of this government has always been directed toward big financial interests, never in favour of the Canadian people. Seventy five per cent of the Canadian trade policy has been directed toward the marketing of western wheat while other farm products of eastern Canada have been completely ignored by this government. That is why provincial governments, and more particularly the government of the province of Quebec, are more than ever entitled to question the policy of the federal government in those fields, and I am more and more convinced that provincial governments are right in wanting to assume responsibilities for those fields because the federal government refused to do its duty.

This is the budget: a statistical hoax, an illusory description of the situation and a few favours granted to Great Britain; tax abatements for people in higher brackets, a stronger control of big financial interests over our economy, astronomical payments of a colonial tribute to foreign capitalism and, for the people, a few crumbs to keep them quiet.
Like the vanquished of Gaul in Caesar's time who had to crawl under the Caudine forks, the Minister of Finance subjects the Canadian people to the control of high finance.
What has been overlooked is to give back Canada to Canadians. What has been overlooked is to enable private individuals and families to enjoy prosperity, to develop our social institutions in the fields of leisure, education and so on. Let us recognize this potential. Let us recognize at the same time the needs of our country, of our citizens, of the whole world, and then, with the use of progressive and drastic measures, we will know a true economic progress, not for England, not for the big shots but for each and every one of the Canadian citizens.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is the first occasion I have had the privilege of participating in a budget debate and I would hope that the House might welcome the introduction of a small measure of virginity into this controversial issue. It is always a pleasure, of course, to follow the hon. Member for Lapointe (Mr. Gregoire) because he seems to enjoy himself so much in any debate. I propose, however, first of all to deal with some of the criticisms directed from across the floor by the financial critic of the Official Opposition, the hon. Member for Digby-Anna-polis-Kings (Mr. Nowlan). I wish to assure the hon. Member that we on this side of the House have a very warm regard for him, but I am sure he will not take it amiss if I say that that regard does not extend to the acceptance of his judgment on economic matters.
It was rather significant that the chief financial critic did not go into any analysis in depth of economic conditions in the country today, although the occasion was rather appropriate and he had ample opportunity to do so. I suggest that the answer is very simple, namely the general satisfaction with economic conditions in Canada today. His chief criticism, Mr. Speaker, which was not of a wounding nature, centred around the fact that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) had not seen fit to remove the sales tax upon production machinery and equipment. The hon. Member attempted to fortify his argument by leaning upon a statement-I will not say a
April 29, 1965

The Budget-Mr. Pennell self-serving statement-issued by the Canadian Manufacturers' Association on April 10 last. I might say that the nakedness of the argument put forward by the hon. Member is found in his own quotation. I therefore do not hesitate to put that quotation on the record again. I quote:
New manufacturing investment in the Canadian economy in 1965 is forecast to exceed $2.2 billion, a sum never before equalled in a single year. It is 23 per cent greater than the $1.8 billion invested last year and two thirds as much again as the $1.3 billion of 1963.
I might add, Mr. Speaker, that this is typical of the confidence of Canadian businessmen in the present administration. I do not wish to do an injustice to the hon. Member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings inasmuch as the fact is that he went on to introduce a qualifying paragraph which I will also put on the record. In this regard he referred to the anticipated tax reduction on production machinery and equipment.
Should these expectations not be realized, there could very well be a distinct scaling down in capital investment intentions to the detriment of the economy and government revenues alike.
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that the hon. Member has obviously forgotten to look at the record of achievement in 1964 because this is the same doleful prophecy we have heard for the last two years. The record will show that investment in 1964 was $500 million more than in 1963. However, the hon. Member sought to bolster his position with further quotations and one to which he referred was a statement by the President of Chemcell to a meeting of company shareholders. It is to be found on page 699 of Hansard of yesterday. Again the hon. Member was referring to the failure to reduce or remove the tax on production machinery and equipment, and he implied that this would be a great brake on Canadian exports. Again, in fairness to him I give the quotation:
This tax is a serious brake on national progress... Only the general level of Canadian prosperity has concealed the Innate viciousness of this tax...
It is rather remarkable, Mr. Speaker, that the quotation referred to by the hon. Member mentions the general level of Canadian prosperity.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I find the hon. Member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings much more attractive when he remains cheerful, as he is now. However, I would suggest that if the hon. Member had made even a cursory examina-

tion of the figures to be found in the White Paper he would have found the answer to the question he posed. The latest D.B.S. figures for exports of inedible end products, which consist mainly of manufactured goods, are as follows: In 1963 exports amounted to $779 million while in 1964 they amounted to $1,109 million, an increase of $330 million or more than 40 per cent in exports of Canadian manufactured goods to foreign countries. If the hon. Member will look at the record he will see that the evidence of our economy is clear and compelling.
I would suggest to those who are concerned about the economic future of the country that the production of steel is one of the most accurate barometers of the future. Since there is a great propensity for quoting statements from various newspapers, may I say that I think the Financial Post put the situation rather well on the 10th of April when it stated:
The Canadian steelmakers are hurrying a new expansion program that will boost capacity by at least one third during the next five years. Total capital outlay will be about $750 million, steel authorities told the Financial Post this week. Expansion programs are being tailored to a forecasted annual growth in steel markets of 7.5 per cent to 1970. Expansion plans have been speeded up because steelmakers badly underestimated market growth-it was longer and stronger than they figured-in recent years, and we are now about one million tons short in productive capacity.
All this reflects the confidence that this administration has restored to Canada's economy, and I do not think we can overemphasize the cumulative and far reaching effect that confidence can have in restoring and maintaining the economy.
The very satisfactory condition of our monetary reserves in gold and foreign exchange again is most cogent evidence that this Government and this country command the respect of investors both at home and abroad.
I do not propose to shirk other issues raised by the hon. Member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings. I am going to turn now to the tax reduction. I say openly and frankly that the benefit of the tax reduction, which applies to the great majority of taxpayers, was a modest one. But, Mr. Speaker, if you are going to put the tax reduction in its proper perspective you must weigh the total impact it is going to have on the economy. The real test of the budget is whether the tax reduction will meet the fundamental necessity of moving our economy forward, and without inflation. If the economy becomes stagnant,
April 29, 1965	COMMONS
then no matter what tax reduction is made all will suffer. If we are able to keep the economy moving forward at its present rate of growth, all will gain.
I should like to put it on the record, Mr. Speaker, that in large measure it was the fiscal policies introduced by the present Minister of Finance that made it possible for us to introduce a tax reduction at this time without impairing the Canadian economy. In many ways the present budget is a complement to the budget of 1964. The fiscal policies introduced at that time enabled the Government to reduce the budgetary deficit to $83 million in 1964 from $690 million in the fiscal year 1962-63. The Minister of Finance knew that new policies had to be introduced to meet the challenge of unemployment, and it is within the recollection of the House that when he brought in his new policy of tax incentives there was considerable controversy, particularly because hon. Members across the floor were advocating then as they do today that we follow in the footsteps of the United States with regard to tax reductions. It is worthy of note, Mr. Speaker, that the over-all performance of the Canadian economy in 1964 was considerably better than that of the United States.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
Now, Mr. Speaker, I have said that the tax reduction was a modest one in many instances. I am not going to evade the issue. I agree that the greatest direct benefit is conferred on taxpayers who are carrying the greatest share of the tax burden. This is inevitable, and follows when you have a general tax reduction across the board in the standard rate. The Minister realized, and he made it clear, that we were not sounding a note of self-satisfaction; there was no room for complacency. Although the economy is sound, and although it is on a firmer base than it has been for many years, although we can expect continued advances, there is room for improvement. The Minister felt it was necessary that we should step up our consumer spending, particularly with the increased production coming out of expanded capital investment. It is, I think, generally recognized that a tax reduction is one way of stepping up and expanding the economy.
At the same time it must be borne in mind that the closer we move toward a full economy, the greater the danger of inflation. So the question of a tax reduction becomes a matter of judgment. No Minister, no matter how long he looks at all the figures, all the 22620-482
DEBATES	743
The Budget-Mr. Pennell forecasts, all the estimates, can do other than finally fall back on the question of judgment. The margin of error in this judgment is very great. I should like to put before you what I believe to be a very strong illustration. If there is a change of 1 per cent in the spending or saving habits of the Canadian people, it could make a difference of $360 million as to whether the money goes into consumer spending or is retained as savings. Let us remember that a change of 1 per cent can make a difference of $360 million in the disposition of the personal income of the Canadian people. I submit therefore, as there is no precise mathematical formula upon which the Minister can rely, he has to fall back on his own judgment. I say, with great respect, when we look back on the past achievements of the Canadian economy we are entitled to rely upon his judgment with the fullest confidence.
The total tax reduction amounts in a year to approximately $265 million. It is expected that this tax reduction, which will take the form of an increase in personal disposable income, will be spent and respent and by circulating through the economy it will generate spending capital in an amount greater than the original tax cut. Of course, it has to be recognized that there will be a decline immediately in Government revenues. It is to be hoped also, Mr. Speaker, that with an expanded economy there will be a feed back in revenues, with a substantial beneficial effect on our budgetary position, provided of course expenditures are held at the proper level. My interpretation of the budget is that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) took the necessary steps to step up or to bring into the economy the consumer spending required to assist the increased production we are setting from our expanded capital investment. I respectfully submit that this is a balance approach to our economic problems and to the present needs of our economy.
I propose now, Mr. Speaker, to deal with the subamendment proposed by the hon. Member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Cameron). I do hope that the hon. Member, who is temporarily absent, will believe in my sincerity when I say that I have a high respect for his opinions and for him personally. However, I say to him, and I trust he will acquit me of incivility, if I say that if the N.D.P. really wants to be taken seriously as an alternative to Government it must face with more responsibility the fiscal consequences of what it proposes. The Minister of Finance has already spoken
April 29, 1365

The Budget-Mr. Pennell in this debate and has supplied me with some figures. It would be most instructive, Mr. Speaker, to examine the consequences of the proposals contained in the subamendment. The proposal to raise the personal income tax exemption by $500 for single persons and $1,000 for married persons and to raise the old age security payment to $100 per month, would cost $1,150 million per annum. If the hon. Member intended that the $100 per month under the old age security was to be paid at age 65, as his party proposed in the last session, then the total national bill would be $1,790 million per annum.
Let us consider the smaller of these two sums. It is proposed that we add $1,150 million per annum to Government expenditures. I respectfully suggest that it was quite out of character and quite unworthy of the hon. Member, for whom I have high regard, to move the subamendment without indicating precisely how this huge sum would be financed. Does he seriously suggest that it should be added to the deficit at a time when our resources are being used to a fuller extent than has been the case for years? If this is the proposal, it would certainly be a sure way of raising prices and I am sure that no party in this House wants that.
If, on the other hand, the N.D.P. has in mind covering this extra national expenditure of $1,150 million by increasing some other form of taxation, then I submit it was incumbent upon the hon. Members to be more precise and to say which taxes he would propose to increase. By way of example, I say that to collect another $1,150 million through the sales tax, would require increasing the rate from 11 per cent to 18 per cent. Is that what the hon. Member wants? Unless the N.D.P. is prepared to state clearly how much is involved in terms of additional expenditure and how the amount is to be raised, then it must forgive people both inside and outside this House for regarding the subamendment as one of pure, political expediency.
Let me put some more figures on the record, Mr. Speaker. The proposal for an extra $1,150 million of expenditure, in terms of corporate income tax, would mean adding an extra 24 per cent tax on corporations. The lower rate of tax would become 45 per cent and the top rate would be 74 per cent. Perhaps I might lower the temperature of the debate, Mr. Speaker, if I turn to another proposal in the budget, but perhaps it would be better if I called it five o'clock.

subtopic: LAURENTIDE BANK OF CANADA
LAURENTIDE BANK OF CANADA
speechtext:
The capital of the new bank is to be $30,000,000 divided into 3,000,000 shares. The Banking and Commerce committee will be able to examine the plans for sale and distribution of these shares in detail. It will see that through the proposed distribution to the widely dispersed and varied existing Canadian shareholders of Laurentide Finance to the extent of 47 per cent and through underwriters to the general public to the extent of 53 per cent, the shareholders of the new bank will represent a wide and varied segment of the investing public and that control of the bank will not rest with any small group of people or corporations. I want to say now, however, that the new bank will not be a subsidiary of Power Corporation or of the Laurentide Financial Corporation. And, in answer to questions asked last session, it will not be the retail outlet for Laurentide Finance.
Clause 5 of the Bill is a special clause which provides first that the directors of the bank shall be Canadians and, second, that at least 90 per cent of the shareholders of the bank shall be Canadian. This anticipates legislation announced by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon).
You will note from the Bill, Mr. Speaker, that the head office of the Laurentide Bank shall be in Vancouver; that six of its provisional directors are from British Columbia and two are from the City of Montreal. It is intended that the bank shall be thoroughly national in character. It is obvious that any new national bank must start from some regional base, as did our existing chartered banks, and therefore the first branches will be opened in and around the two cities of Vancouver and Montreal, where the provisional directors reside. It is intended eventually, as conditions warrant, to provide a general banking service throughout Canada. It is because the head office will be in Vancouver and the principal management will be located there that I am proud to associate myself with this Bill and with the incorporation of the Laurentide Bank of Canada.
Without being critical of the existing banks, I am aware of the difficulty which Western Canadians face in capital formation. In the West, and in British Columbia particularly, we have a fast growing and developing region, a boom area, yet not one chartered bank has seen fit to have a head office West of Toronto-a head office and financial policy oriented to the special needs and problems of Western Canada. We in British Columbia have long felt the need of establishing finan-
Private Bills
cial institutions that are oriented to our special needs and problems, and I would hope that no one in this House would stand in the way of helping to fill this need for British Columbia.
Many Members are not familiar with the tremendous developments going on west of the Rockies. Some have said that all financial institutions must be centred in Eastern Canada. One only need go to San Francisco to see that in the Western United States financial institutions have been formed and have been able to grow to national importance. Vancouver, I like to think, is the San Francisco of Canada, and we are at the stage where we want, we need and we are able to support Western financial and banking institutions.
The other region of Canada to be immediately served by this bank is the Province of Quebec. There are two leading French speaking Canadians on the Board of Directors. Laurentide Financial Corporation has carried on business in the Province of Quebec for a long and, I think, happy period. I trust Members from Quebec, all eager to see the further development of their Province, as I am of mine, will recognize the value of creating additional banking facilities within their Province to contribute to the economic development of Quebec.
Some Members have raised the question of whether or not Canada needs additional chartered banks. Members of the Banking Committee will want to examine this question in detail. Briefly, however, I would refer Members to the Royal Commission on Banking -the Porter Report-which makes it clear throughout that in the opinion of the Commission, there is no hazard to Canada's chartered banking system by the incorporation of additional chartered banks. The Porter Report has recommended a more open and competitive banking system. It has referred to the dangers of undue concentration in our banking system. I quote very briefly from page 362 of the report, where it states:
There must be sufficient competition among these Institutions that borrowers and savers have alternatives open to them.
If it is felt the incorporation of an additional bank would endanger the Canadian banking system, one of the finest in the world, any of the existing banks or the Canadian Bankers' Association had the full right and opportunity to come before the Senate Committee last session and say so. They did not. Our Canadian bankers believe, like most Members of this House, in the free enterprise system; they believe that the very essence of

April 29, 1965
Private Bills
that system is the free play of competitive forces. We do not believe in the stifling of competition. Surely we cannot believe that our banking system should be left static, ultimately by way of merger and take-over to fall into the hands of two or three chartered banks. In the last ten years alone the number of banks has decreased from eleven to eight. This process should not be allowed to continue.
There are those in the House, of course, who do not believe in the free enterprise system. There are those in the House who want to make drastic and sweeping changes in the banking system. But surely they too must feel that increased competition within the banking system can only be helpful. Surely they are not going to use their position in this House to prevent the passage of a Bill which would result in protecting the existing chartered banks from further and desirable competition, and give the existing banks a monopoly over Canadian banking business.
There are those who point to the number of branches we have in Canada and say that the number is ample and sufficient for the needs of Canada. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that it is not sufficient to say we have so many branches, and that is enough. Surely a bank is and must be a policy-making financial institution whose services may be offered by one branch or by a thousand branches. An abundance of branches is nothing more than a convenient extension of services, not an extension of policy.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
A bank, no matter how many hundreds or even thousands of branches it may have in operation, is one bank, having one policy, paying one rate to its depositors and demanding one rate from any particular class of borrower. This policy is formulated at head office and simply implemented by the large number of branch managers, and there is certainly not one policy for each branch, but one for the entire structure.
In Canada we have now shrunk to the point where, other than in Quebec and small portions of Ontario and the Maritimes, there are only six chartered banks, and I include the Mercantile Bank in this number. In British Columbia we have only six, and in Alberta only five. To me, it is self-evident that the person proposing to transact banking business, and having eight alternative policymaking financial institutions to which to turn, obviously is better served than the Albertan or British Columbian, who is limited to five

or six. To me it is obvious that an increase in the number of chartered banks, thus providing to Canadians and the Canadian economy additional policy-making financial institutions, additional head offices, can only be of benefit to the growth and development of our economy.
Another argument raised against incorporating banks at this point is that they should be made to wait for the decennial revision of the Bank Act. There are many answers to this argument. The Mercantile Bank of Canada, the last bank chartered in Canada, was chartered in 1953, immediately before the then decennial revision of the Bank Act. Second, the sponsors of, and investors in, this proposed new bank are aware that the Bank Act is due for revision. Any new bank will, of course, be subject to any new revisions made to the Bank Act. The sponsors and investors are prepared to go ahead in the knowledge that the Bank Act will be shortly revised. Surely if they are prepared to go ahead in the face of possible amendments, they should, other things being equal, be allowed to do so.
Whether to incorporate this bank, or any other bank, one must apply the standards laid out by the Minister of Finance in this House many months ago; namely, is it properly financed? I say, Mr. Speaker, that the Laurentide Bank of Canada, with a proposed capitalization of $30 million, with the support that it will obtain from Laurentide Finance Corporation and the general public, is properly financed. Is it supported by financially responsible people? In my brief outline of the sponsors of this Bill I have indicated that they are financially responsible people with wide and varied experience in the business life of their communities. The Laurentide Bank of Canada is assured of a broad and diversified ownership, and its backers have the resources and the experience to ensure that it will be financially sound. Will control of the bank remain in Canadian hands? Yes, Mr. Speaker, by reason of section 5 that will be so. I suggest that the Laurentide Bank of Canada meets all of these conditions, and careful scrutiny by the members of the Banking and Commerce Committee will satisfy them that the Laurentide Bank should be incorporated.
Now, Mr. Speaker, this and other Bills of a similar nature were introduced during the last session. This particular Bill was given first reading in the Senate on March 24, 1964. It was given second reading and referred to Committee on May 13, referred back from
April 29, 1965

Committee on July 27, and given third reading in the other place on July 28. In this House it was given first reading and reported from the other place on July 29, 1964. It was introduced for second reading and debate commenced on October 15, 1964. Debate took place on October 15 and resumed on November 12, 1964, and February 25, 1965. Thereafter it did not come up for debate again, and died on the Order Paper at the end of last session without having been referred to the Banking and Commerce Committee.
This session the Bill, as hon. Members will note, has been presented and introduced in the House of Commons first. I can appreciate and understand the desire of Members of this House to very carefully examine proposals to incorporate a new bank. I suggest that the proper place for questions to be asked and explanations given is the Banking and Commerce Committee of this House. If, following the appearance of the sponsors of this bank and the giving of explanations by them, some Members of the House have objections to the incorporation of this new bank, they have their rights and remedies and can act accordingly. But I would hope, Mr. Speaker, that progress, or the lack of progress, of this Bill is not going to be linked to the progress, or lack of progress, of any other banking proposals that may be made by others and that may particularly be made by the Premier of the Province of British Columbia. Whether this bank should be allowed to carry on business is one question. Whether Premier Bennett, or any other Provincial Government for that matter, should be allowed to carry on a banking business is quite another and entirely separate question. May I say at the outset that I am not in favour of this process of incorporating banks. Similarly I am not in favour of using this process to incorporate any other business in Canada. I think this procedure is a holdover from some time in antiquity in England when nearly everything of this nature was done by way of petitioning for a private bill to incorporate groups of people to do various things. I suggest that when and if the Min-

ister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) gets around to introducing a revised Bank Act or amendments thereto-for it is my understanding that it is because of the provision in the Bank Act that Bills to incorporate banks must be done by this method-he should remove this provision, because I think it is a waste of the time of Parliament, which periodically has to concern itself with one small section of a particular part of the economy, or one or two companies within a certain part of the economy, subject them to debate and examination, while at the same time-

I am not familiar with the process of renewal charters of banks, but I assume that if there is to be a regular decennial consideration of the Bank Act in its entirety, then that should be sufficient for the renewal of charters. But as I say, I am not familiar with the actual process.
If I was not clear, what I am saying in essence is that I do not think the Parliament of Canada is the place to incorporate private businesses in this country. Private businesses should be incorporated outside of the Parliament of Canada under the Bank Act, or the Companies Act, or the various financial or trust company acts, or whatever particular statute applies. We should not be bothered with this sort of thing. However we are bothered with it; it is before us and we must concern ourselves with it. I hope to direct my remarks to the concern we have particularly with respect to the Laurentide Bank, the Bill to incorporate which is before us, as well as the relationship of this bank with other banks, and I hope I will be permitted to cover similar ground to that covered by the sponsor of the Bill.
The hon. Member went into great detail and almost eulogized the free enterprise system in talking about competition, seeming
April 29, 1965

thereby to indicate that there has been in years gone by a lessening of competition in the banking field, and that the incorporation of the Laurentide Bank and other banks will increase this so-called competition in the banking field. It is true that in the past number of years there have been consolidations or mergers of banks, which procedure has in fact reduced the number of banks in existence in Canada. If the Bill presently before us and that relating to the Bank of Western Canada are passed, and those companies commence operations, this will in fact increase the number of chartered banks in Canada. It does not follow from this, however, that there will be any increase in competition, because as far as I have been able to assess the information there is no competition in the banking field.
The banks of Canada operate as a very tightly run oligopoly within which there is no difference of opinion, and no difference of approach. The banks are regulated to a large extent by the Bank Act, and by the Bank of Canada in the manner in which they do business. They are restricted as to the amount of reserves they can have, and they are regulated as to the amount of interest they can charge, and the like. I do not know one bank which offers any large degree of competition over that offered by another bank, unless it happens to be in the form of the friendly smile of the manager or of the accountant responsible for granting loans. But that is the extent of the competition-a competition by front, competition by a smile, competition by a pleasant personality.
Competition in the true sense of the word, by way of providing a service or a product to the general public which is the best possible and at the lowest possible price, just does not exist in the banking institutions of Canada. The incorporation of Laurentide Bank will not increase competition but will merely add one other company to the chain of companies already members of the banking oligopoly, and no one will notice the difference except, perhaps, that some additional money will be expended to build offices in Vancouver, presumably Montreal, and other parts of the country in which it wishes to set up branches. Therefore when one talks about the degree of competition in the banking field in Canada, I think he is talking about something which does not exist, because there is no such animal.
If there is the desire to inject some competition, some factor relating thereto, or to re-
Private Bills
strict or control the monopoly or oligopoly positions of chartered banks in Canada, then I submit that the way to do it is through the Bank Act or through the Combines Investigation Act. The Combines Investigation Act is a law of Canada which prohibits price fixing, mergers and monopolies which have a bad influence on the economy of the nation. However, banks are excluded from the provisions of the Combines Investigation Act. Banks can merge. They can fix prices and do all the things, for instance, that the oil industry cannot do. They can do all of these criminal acts-criminal for other companies-and are completely exempted from prosecution under the Combines Investigation Act for criminal activity.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
If there is the desire to bring some degree of competition to bear on the banking industry, which is the principal base of the Combines Investigation Act, then I submit that my hon. friend's government should have spent their time in the last couple of years in bringing about suggested changes to the Combines Investigation Act so that this very competition could be brought about. But they have sought to ignore that approach. Whether or not the Minister of Finance will introduce any amendments to the Bank Act, which in effect will incorporate provisions similar to those contained within the Combines Investigation Act, remains to be seen. The way is open for the Government to deal with monopolies and closely tied control, such as exists in the banking industry in Canada. They can do so by creating the so-called forces of competition in this field by way of amendment to the Bank Act. I doubt very much whether the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) will take advantage of this opportunity because he does not believe in doing things in that way. I do not believe this Government believes in doing things that way either.
To cite an example, several years ago Canadian Breweries was charged under the Combines Investigation Act with engaging in a merger or an operation detrimental to the best interests of Canada. That firm was prosecuted by the Minister of Justice, Mr. Davie Fulton, of the previous Government. Incidentally, Mr. Speaker, I understand that hon. Gentleman wishes to return to this place to carry on in the same manner as he did when he was here.
The case against Canadian Breweries under the Combines Investigation Act was lost by the prosecution. I understand that the case

April 29. 1965
Private Bills
was heard by Chief Justice McBuer of the Ontario Supreme Court. His judgment in effect stated that Canadian Breweries, and other breweries in Ontario, were governed so far as the price of beer was concerned by provincial laws and regulations, and therefore could not do any serious damage to the interests of the general public by reason of a merger.
It is my submission that banks are in a position that they can do as they wish in this field of operation, and operate a closely knit oligopoly to the disadvantage of the public, and solely in the interests of the banking institution. There is no competition in this field, and those who think there is or will be by increasing the number of chartered banks, are thinking in nonsensical ways or using cliches to make the situation sound reasonable.
It is not my suggestion that the hon. Member who is the sponsor of this Bill is not acting with sincerity. He speaks in glowing terms of the individuals connected with this proposed bank and uses phrases associated with free enterprise and competition to support this proposition. He probably believes in what he has said, but I suggest he is deluded in this regard, just as the Party to which he belongs is deluded.
An increase in the number of banking institutions in this country, such as the Lau-rentide Bank, the incorporation of which is being sought by this Bill, will not increase competition in this field of banking. Following the incorporation of such a bank I am sure it will make as much profit as possible, as quickly as possible, and become an associated brother in the Canadian Banking Association. Once that took place there would be no change whatever in the existing situation. One more bank would be in existence, with several branches, but there would be no increase in competition.
I think we must refer to what happened in this regard during the last Session of Parliament. During that Session proceedings were instituted in the Senate for the incorporation of the Laurentide Bank, the Bank of Western Canada and the Bank of British Columbia. What happened at that time should be referred to in order to make very clear what our position is in respect of these sought for incorporations. During the last Session the Senate put into operation whatever machinery it has to give its blessing to the Bank of Western Canada and the Laurentide Bank. It did not, however, give a similar blessing to the pro-

posed Bank of British Columbia, but saw fit to reject that particular Bill on the grounds that it is not wise for provincial governments to invest money in privately chartered banks.
That principle was subsequently echoed by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon), when Parliament reconvened following the Christmas recess, when he said that it was the policy of this Government to introduce legislation to revise the Bank Act. Presumably that legislation will be placed before us within a few months, and it will prohibit governments from investing money in banks chartered under the Bank Act, and prohibits provincial governments, which invest money in the share structure of such banks before the Bank Act is revised, from owning voting shares. Presumably that was the principle followed by the Senate when it rejected the Bill in respect of the British Columbia Bank.
A certain responsibility rests now on the promoters of the Bank of British Columbia which, so far as I am concerned, they must meet if they are still interested in promoting that Bank. I am not advancing any argument on their behalf, and it is their business to present a petition to Parliament in this regard, but it is my understanding that if they intend to do so they must do so by May 17, which is the deadline for the presentation of petitions for private bills.
With all due respect to the eloquent argument made by the sponsor of this Bill, I do not believe we should proceed with it before May 17, because at that time we will then know whether or not the promoters of the British Columbia Bank intend to discharge their responsibility by reintroducing such a petition, as has been done in respect of the Laurentide Bank and the Bank of Western Canada. It is my submission that we should consider these three propositions as a unit in so far as Parliament is concerned, and that we should delay consideration of the Bill now before us at least until we know whether the promoters of the Bank of British Columbia intend to ask for the incorporation of that institution. At that time we can proceed with all three petitions, or, if the promoters of that Bank decide not to seek incorporation, we can deal with the petitions in respect of the Laurentide Bank and the Bank of Western Canada on their individual merits.
It is my impression that the promoters of the Bank of British Columbia based their petition for incorporation on an expressed desire by the Government of the Province of
April 29, 1965

British Columbia to invest a certain amount of money in the share capital of such a bank. Any hope in this regard has been put aside, at least temporarily, by the declaration of the Minister of Finance to the effect that the promoters or sponsors of the Bank of British Columbia may find it necessary to revise the capital structure of their proposed bank.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
This may be the reason for their delay in presenting a petition to Parliament for the incorporation of the Bank of British Columbia. But because it was the present Government that decided to change the rules and move the goal posts in the midst of the incorporation proceedings respecting three banks, I believe that Parliament should give the promoters of the Bank of British Columbia the benefit of the doubt and delay consideration of these bills until the 17th of May. If at that time there is a petition before Parliament for the incorporation of the Bank of British Columbia, we will be able to proceed to deal with it and with the charters now before us.
No petition may be made. Quite frankly, knowing Premier Bennett as I do, I doubt that he will want to proceed as he originally planned. He probably has some other trick up his sleeve, such as a reference to the Supreme Court of Canada. However, if by the 17th of May the promoters of the Bank of British Columbia have not presented a petition it is of no more concern to the Parliament of Canada and we will merely proceed at that time with the business at hand, the Bill to incorporate Laurentide Bank of Canada and the Bill to incorporate the Bank of Western Canada. It would be desirable then to accede to the appeal of the hon. Member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. Basford), take the Bills at face value, examine their relationships to the banking institutions of Canada and the value they might have to Western Canada and generally deal with them on their merits. It is only a matter of a couple of weeks, however, and I submit it would be appropriate for Parliament to give the Bank of British Columbia the benefit of the doubt and hope they will accept their responsibility and meet the deadline. I see you rising, Mr. Speaker, so I assume my deadline has been reached.

Mr. Speaker, in speaking to the bill before us may I say I am certainly in agreement with what the hon. Member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) said concerning competition in the banking business. The fact remains that in my opinion there is no real competition in the banking business. As the hon. Member pointed out, it is a matter of the personalities of the bank manager and the accountants with whom the individual deals. I think one receives basically the same service from any chartered bank.
Since we are talking about incorporating banks, there is one point I think should be brought to the attention of the House at this time. Here we have a company, ostensibly a finance company, that now wishes to go into the banking business. It is known that at those times when the country is faced with a tight money policy there are certain leaks in the case of finance companies. When a tight money policy is going to be introduced it affects the line of credit that a particular bank will give to an individual who wishes to borrow money, and prior to the tight money policy coming into effect we find the strange situation of finance companies upping their line of credit to a great degree. This puts them in the advantageous position of being able to service the customer with money that rightfully he should have been able to get from a bank in the first place at 6 per cent, but for which he now has to pay up to 24 per cent interest.
When a tight money policy has been in effect many a person has gone to a bank to borrow money only to be told that, while he has a wonderful financial statement and ordinarily the bank could lend him such and such a sum of money on the basis of that statement, his line of credit limits him to so many dollars because the bank is operating under a tight money policy. Because he has already made use of that much credit he is told by the bank that they are sorry there is no money available for him, but if he will go across the street to such and such finance company they will certainly look after him. The finance companies are able to do so because they have been tipped off ahead of time and have raised their line of credit to the point where they can borrow from the banking system the very money that the individual should have been entitled to borrow from the bank.
This is only one phase of what we are up against so far as our banking institutions are concerned. There is the other matter of the direct creation of credit, which is an important feature. When we say that the banks are limited in what they can lend, this is not exactly so. Actually they are not limited, because by the purchase of Government bonds and other gilt-edged securities they can then use these securities to establish credit with the Bank of Canada and, having acquired credit with the Bank of Canada, can legally multiply their loans twelve and a half times, and under suasion generally about six times. [DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
This, of course, means there is a tremendous advantage to banks. You all have had the experience of going into a bank and some bank clerk has said to you, "We are on a tight money policy; we are borrowing our money at 6 per cent and we are lending it to you at 6 per cent. How do you expect us to exist?". This just is not so. For every dollar the bank would borrow from the Central Bank, it is able to lend out at least six times that amount, under what we call suasion, or up to 12 times under what we have set as the legal limit. The fact remains that the ratio was set from between 3 per cent and 12 per cent, but the Bank of Canada has never enforced the 12 per cent equity provision so far as deposit liabilities are concerned from the chartered banks.
We say, therefore, there is a lot more to the functions of banking than just going in and making deposits and then writing out cheques. We believe that the time has come when the banking institutions of this country should be given a much broader base upon which they can provide industrial capital. We believe that in Canada we have one of the best banking systems in the world today. There are certain limitations, and there are certain functions of the banks that we believe should be corrected. We believe also that the Central Bank should take its place, along with the present banking system, to round out the total amount of banking facilities that are absolutely necessary to equate the purchasing power of the nation with its productive capacity. Until this is done all the noise about the war on poverty will be just so many idle words. In my view we must come to the point where we recognize that we have to finance production and consumption in this country. The financing of production will be done through the industrial sector or the private sector and the financing, to a certain point,

April 29, 1965

of consumption that is necessary will have to be done through the public sector; in other words the Bank of Canada and the Government of the day. There is a way in which industrial expansion takes place without the banking institutions of this country. The people who are interested in the development of natural resources go outside of the country to get banking services. The banks of the United States, Belgium and France can monetize a prospectus which the banking institutions of this country, by law, cannot do.
I can give you an example. I come from a timber country. If some individual had a licence to cut timber and there was a good potential market for the material he would produce, a bank outside of Canada can monetize that prospectus, take security on the assets as they develop. In Canada today this is not possible under our banking system. The banks, themselves, cannot give that type of service. What do we find? We find a good many of our industries becoming controlled by people outside of Canada because of the lack of facilities in Canada.
Before I take my seat, Mr. Speaker, I want to make it abundantly clear that I am in accord so far as the proposed adoption of this Bill on second reading is concerned. However, I should like to see this Bill complete its passage through second reading of the House, and that we give the same recognition to the Bank of British Columbia, a Bill for the establishment of which I expect a bill will be introduced before long. I hope that application will receive exactly the same treatment. I do not believe for one moment that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) can give us any real ground for saying that control of 10 per cent of the shares of any bank gives control of that bank. Some time, perhaps during the Budget debate, I should like him to answer that question. I do not believe he can prove in any way, shape or form that this is a fact. We feel that, in principle, we can use more banking services. We do not believe this is going to make money any cheaper, but we do believe that there is room for more banking services in the country.
I believe it is six o'clock, and perhaps you would call it six o'clock, Mr. Speaker.

The Budget-Mr. Pennell turn to what might perhaps be considered the less controversial aspects of the budget. I do not propose to stand at any length between the hon. Member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Hamilton) and the House, but perhaps I may be allowed to make a personal observation. It was with a great sense of personal satisfaction that I noticed the Minister of Finance had made provision for the introduction of a measure to prevent waste products polluting our streams and waters. I make bold to point out that in the course of my maiden speech in this house some three years ago I made a similar proposal, and it is pleasant to reflect that patience has its own reward and that my plea did not fall upon deaf ears. I am sure this proposal commands the universal support of hon. Members, because it seems to me it makes only common sense that, while we can, we should attempt to prevent the pollution of our streams and waters, one of our most precious assets, rather than attempt to cure pollution after it has taken place.
I wish to say a word or two about the proposal to continue the accelerated depreciation allowance. Once again I believe I am on solid ground when I say that the House generally will support this measure. In this age of rapid technological advance a manufacturer must think not only in terms of the original cost of a piece of machinery; he must also bear in mind the possibility that he may have to replace it within a year or so because, though it is still physically sound, it has become out of date. I agree with the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings (Mr. Nowlan) that we must make every endeavour to remain competitive. If industry goes along using out of date machinery it may well be doing so at the price of increasing the cost of production and decreased productivity. It seems to me only fair and proper that we should stand behind measures which are taken to speed up production and increase productivity.
Finally I should like to say a word about the war on poverty. Let me point out at once that the budget is only one weapon within the arsenal which must be deployed in this formidable task. Poverty cannot be measured only in terms of income. There is poverty of opportunity and poverty of education. I suggest that many of our older citizens are suffering from a poverty of opportunity. While many of them have the ability to work and to get ahead, they are the victims of poverty of opportunity.

speechtext: When I consider the situation of those young people who are dropping out of our secondary schools, it seems to me this represents a failure on the part of our educational system and that these young people will soon suffer as a result of the poverty of their education. The Minister of Finance told us frankly that we must concern ourselves with the training of our young people. Already this Government has devoted approximately $100 million annually to assisting the technical and vocational training program. In addition, youth allowances will cost approximately $46,500,000 during the coming year. We are now awaiting the report of a committee which is inquiring into university finances and I am confident this Government will take action in the wake of that report.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What about the 10,000 scholarships?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Though there is a year of solid achievement behind this budget, no budget of itself can long sustain vigorous and healthy economic progress. That depends on the response we get from all our people from industry, from labour, from management and from the farmers. I recognize, though, that the primary responsibility rests with the Government. I suppose no hon. Member, least of all myself, or no Minister in this House, would claim he has a monopoly of knowledge on economic and fiscal matters, but I humbly suggest that the present Budget will meet the purpose for which it is created, that is, to sustain a healthy rate of economic growth.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am
very pleased that the Parliamentary Secretary should have chosen to say something about the difficulty attached to use by Governments of the monetary structure we have built into
April 29, 1965

the framework of our over-all management of the people's affairs. I am glad he raised this point, because the first subject I intend to deal with tonight is this question of inflationary dangers.
Before I proceed to do so, perhaps I may list the other three subjects on which I intend to speak, so as to give an idea of the scope of my remarks. The second subject I propose to deal with is the failure of the Government to give real support to the National Economic Council. My third point concerns the absence from the budget of either long term or short term objectives. The fourth is the Government's failure to support trade expansion in a real way.
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)
The first of these subjects, the danger of inflation, is related to the other three, and to indicate the background I should like to describe briefly the main features of what has been happening in the last ten years. As everyone knows, there has been a great debate as to the place of the Central Bank in Canada, in relationship to the elected representatives of the people. In the history of this debate, as I see it, I would like to put one or two of the events into perspective. In 1957 and 1960 Canada faced two recessions. These were met, as far as we could meet them, by heavy fiscal expenditures on public works, increased credit for housing, for farmers, for small businessmen-yes, and exports. As I said, these were part of the powers that we had on the fiscal side.
On the monetary side though, as the Porter Royal Commission makes brutally clear, the course of action from 1958 to 1961 tended to be restrictive. If anyone wants to examine the charts and the various reports of the Bank of Canada he will see that the same form of restrictive action was applied against the Government in the years before we took office in 1957. We got it in 1958, 1959 and 1960. Now that the report has made it very clear that the Governor of the Bank of Canada must always bring his policies into conformity with the elected representatives, I think things have moved much more smoothly. This, Mr. Speaker, raises the main issue about which I wish to speak.
During the four years 1959 to 1962 inclusive, facing unemployment and unused capacity in all segments of industry, the fiscal expansion policies of our Government when in power were kept in check by monetary policies, which I think the following figures make clear. As I read these figures,
The Budget-Mr. Hamilton Mr. Speaker, I can collect two or three different columns of figures using different indicators, indicating the various amounts of money and other things that you can call part of the over-all money supply; but just let me give these figures as indicators. In 1956 the total, at the end of the year, of currency and chartered bank deposits was $11 billion; in 1960 it climbed to $13.9 billion. There was a static three-year period, 1958, 1959 and 1960; but last year, in 1964, at the end of the year it had climbed to over $18 billion.
What do these figures indicate? They indicate that in the last two years there has been a much freer use of the money supply to keep the economy moving forward and expanding. I am not quarrelling with that freer use, having been one of those who fought so hard to make it free and to tie it up to the needs of the economy rather than against the needs of the economy. I know how those in charge of this policy were terrified by the inflation after the Second World War; they were terrified of inflation during the Korean War, and they certainly were confused by the great influx of money that came into this country from 1953 to 1956. These fears which they had made them so conscious of inflation that when we were actually facing the opposite of inflation they imposed, in effect, tight money not only on us but on the previous Government at a time when both governments needed help.
1 think that matter has been cleared up by the Porter Royal Commission, and I expect, from looking at the figures I have just quoted, that the present Minister of Finance has had no such trouble as we experienced. The point I want to make, Mr. Speaker, is that during the period we were in office, because of the braking effect of this unused plant capacity, because of the braking effect of the potential productivity in the primary sector, because of the braking effect of the unemployed or the oversupply of employable people, the cost of living, using round figures, increased only by an average of 1 per cent a year during the four years under discussion.
When we got free of these monetary restrictions, particularly with the devaluation of the dollar, these expansion programs yielded big returns. Incidentally, all these charts and indicators go back to February, 1961, even though the devaluation of the dollar did not start until the budget of that summer; all these indicators that still go upwards started
April 29, 1965

The Budget-Mr. Hamilton in the year 1961, and ever since that time we have had an expanding economy. There was hardly a thing mentioned by the Minister of Finance the other night that has had any effect on our economy since that time, and when he mentions loans to university students, that is a perfect example of the type of thing he gave as having helped the upward movement. These loans have been in effect for over a year, and everyone knows this has not changed the economy upwards at all; it has not at any time had any impact upon the economy. But in spite of all the other things the Minister has done, he has not been able to check the advance that we started in 1961.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker-

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I do not take all the credit for our Government, Mr. Speaker, but in the last year we have had-

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speechtext: Go ahead.
