speechtext: I would ask the hon. Gentleman whether he is suggesting that the Government of which he was a Member did not have power over monetary policy.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
As I said in my opening sentence, Mr. Speaker, this is a debate that has been going on for ten years. If the Minister wants to read the record of this debate, it is present in every bank report and the debates of this House for the last ten years. I am simply putting the record in perspective. I want the Minister to listen, because what I have to say to him at the end of my speech will be worth listening to. I did not want to take all the credit for our Government, Mr. Speaker, any more than the Minister of Finance has the right to take any great credit for his Government.
I do want to point out, however, that we have to admit that last year we had an assist from outside Canada in the form of a reduction of taxes in the United States, and since so much of our economy is tied into their economy, their upward boost has helped us a bit.
Now the situation has changed. In almost every industry the capacity of the plant is almost completely utilized. I say this, in spite of the very rosy conclusion in the White Paper, on page (XI) of the Economic Review of 1964. I quote from that page of the Economic Review:
Productive capacities in general appear to be adequate to meet the probable demands. There may be some supply difficulties in specific localities and industries, which a high degree of mobility of both labour and capital would help to relieve.
Then going on a bit:
In these circumstances of productivity improvement and high labour force growth, the increases in output required to meet the demands outlined above are clearly within the growing capacity of the economy.
This is the view of the White Paper; it is not the view of many men engaged in industry in Canada. I am not going to quote the individual companies, because they will be making their views known, I am sure. But there is one writer, who has already been quoted in this debate, Mr. John Meyer of the Montreal Gazette, who had this to say on April 27, 1965:
The weakness in Mr. Gordon's approach is his assumption that an economy already functioning at close to capacity can be further stimulated by a tax reduction without the risk of overheating it.
Then later on:
What is significant is that the factories and mills, in spite of their continually expanded facilities, are running at capacity.
[DOT] (8:20 p.m.)
I would like to place special emphasis in a general way on two or three of these industries. Of greatest significance at the moment is the steel industry. In eight years production has climbed from approximately 4 million tons a year to toward 10 million tons. The industry now faces an immediate building program of approximately $1 billion, and more probably a $10 billion expansion in the long run. Likewise, the pulp and paper industry, one of our leading dollar earners, is engaged in a billion dollar expansion of facilities at the present time. Much more has to be done in increasing production and improving the facilities of moving the raw material to the mills. The petrochemical industries are just coming into a period of tremendous expansion to meet world demand. The same indications for needs of capital expansion are evident in almost all sectors of our private economy. To add to the difficulties, the Canada Pension Plan will withdraw some $400 million a year from the available capital. Also the Government shows no indication of checking the increase of expenditure in the public sector. On the contrary their public timidity is so great that no request is refused or postponed.
Therefore I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that the country now faces a serious threat of inflation. Last year the money supply was increased by $1.5 billion, which is over twice

April 29. 1965	COMMONS
the average rate the previous government was allowed to expand when faced with unemployment and a slowdown in the economy inherited in 1957. The cost of living is now climbing by close to 2 per cent a year and everyone knows what that does to those of low income. More serious than that is the fact that there is no unused plant capacity now to take up the increased consumer demand that there was when we were trying to free the money supply. In respect to that I could quote several authorities from individual businesses.
Now, Mr. Speaker, this budget adds another inflationary force by trying to increase consumer spending. Second, there is a shortage of skilled labour in almost every line of activity, and this produces a cost-push inflation. It is no use telling us that we have 3J per cent of the labour force unemployed. What causes a cost-push inflation is when individual industries, which can be named one after another in the City of Toronto, cannot get enough skilled help to man their factories. In the search for skilled labour you get a pushing upwards of costs, which must eventually go on to the consumer. That is the difference now, compared with what was the case just five years ago.
Third, there is a tremendous need for new capital for plant expansion in the manufacturing industries. The business world is aware of these dangers; the economists are aware of them. Why is the Government not aware of them?
Another point I should like to make tonight is the failure of this budget to support the National Economic Council. In 1962 we proposed that we set up a National Economic Council. The present Government had the honour to carry the legislation into the House and get it through. Their annual review has been published. There is nothing more serious in this budget, Mr. Speaker, than the failure of the Government in departing from the emphasized suggestions of the Economic Council. I should just like to quote a few of the statements from the chapter on implications for policy. First of all, talking about trade agreements, they say:
This conclusion reinforces our conviction that we need a strong and concerted national effort to promote the highest possible gains in productivity and in industrial efficiency-
There is nothing in the Budget to remove the 11 per cent tax, which is a heavy burden on industrial efficiency if we are to move out in competition with the world, not only with
DEBATES	757
The Budget-Mr. Hamilton the industrial nations but with the lower cost producing nations.
The second direction of this policy is stated thus:
In addition, we need a commercial policy directed at securing a substantial improvement in access to foreign markets, coupled with a vigorous program of export promotion, to facilitate the attainment of the required growth of competitive exports.
Where do you find, Mr. Speaker, in the Budget any move to carry out this recommended implication for policy?
Third, again dealing with trade:
New business policies and methods may be needed, as well as a willingness to incur additional risks. Moreover, the need for large increases in exports will be accentuated rather than modified with a more rapid growth of domestic income and demand, and it is crucially important if high employment and dynamic economic growth are to be achieved, that Canadian manufacturing industry should become increasingly export-oriented.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Sharp) says "hear, hear". I will ask him to listen to this part of my remarks-

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I am.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
-because tonight I want to point out that the Minister of Trade and Commerce is no longer riding high in the Cabinet. He has been downgraded, and the man who has gone to the top is one who believes in another philosophy, the Minister of Finance. The interesting thing about the last two years, after the fiasco of the 1963 budget when we saw the Minister of Finance go into eclipse, with all the forces of the business world turned against him, is this: The Government only talks of export drives and measures to help industry. The businessmen hear talk of how Walter has now come back to the leadership of the party in power, and the theme song is: Walter, Walter, lead me to the altar. But we know, Mr. Speaker, why the businessmen are worried. The Government thought they had put up this very bright fellow, the Minister of Trade and Commerce, who was to guide the Cabinet. Now the influence has slid right into the hands of the Minister of Finance again, and this is why the businessmen are worried.
My main charge against the Government and its budget is that it has not paid any attention to the book on economic goals which has just been published. The Government has ignored it. As the hon. Member for Digby-
April 2E'i, 1965

The Budget-Mr. Hamilton Annapolis-Kings (Mr. Nowlan) pointed out yesterday, the Minister has failed to eliminate the tax on production machinery, which would be a major step to increase efficiency. As the same hon. Member said yesterday, the Government has ignored the most pressing problem there is today in Canada-education. He suggested that if they took this $265 million reduction in personal income tax, which does very little for the fellow who saves 3 cents a day, and which does very little for the man making $20,000 a year who saves $600 a year or $50 a month, and used it to cut out the tax on production machinery, then the man saving 3 cents a day would see more jobs available and the man saving $600 a year could even see an extended future. I put it to you, Mr. Speaker, that even though the Government will not remove this 11 per cent tax to save the pride and face of the Minister of Finance, perhaps they will consider throwing this $265 million into education. Not just $1 per capita or something, but throw in the whole works, and do the same next year if the money is available. Education is where the survival of this nation lies. The time for worshipping old myths is past; the time to face new realities is here, and modern education is one reality to be faced.
I mention myths and realities simply to point out that the only trouble with the Minister of Finance, who is a very sincere man, is that he has been brought up on myths which are 60 years out of date. This is what frightens the businessmen. They have now come into the twentieth century and they realize that our policies of expansion are what they wanted. When the Minister brought in his budget in 1963, he carried out exactly what he said he would carry out in his book, at the Kingston Conference and in the Gordon Royal Commission. Before 1963 no one bothered to read the book. But now the businessmen have read "Mein Kampf", they are worried.
Third, trade. Once again may I welcome the Minister of Trade and Commerce to the debate, because it is very clear that the budget speech is not an election speech. You could not get elected to a doghouse with this budget speech. It is certainly not a big factor in the economic policy of the Government. It is certainly not a trade expansion budget. In this respect it ignores completely the suggested policy line of the Economic Council.
[DOT] (8:30 p.m.)
On October 8 last I put forward in this House six proposals on new techniques for

increasing trade. The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Sharp) listened to them, but apparently he has little influence over the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon), who apparently is now restored to popular favour in the Liberal Government. I will again list those six proposals: first, international commodity agreements for products of newly developing nations; second, private international trading companies; third, selling agencies; fourth, purchasing agencies; fifth, an international bank for short term credits; and sixth, growth rate exchanges.
These proposals I have just listed are for consideration. I happen to believe in them, but I admit that they are long-term proposals. They are based on the fact that many of the newly developing nations are state trading nations. They are based on the opinion that to give maximum economic independence from the vertical pull to the south, we have to reach more and more in a horizontal direction to find new and additional markets, not just the United States and European markets. If any of these policies have merit, they were certainly overlooked in the budget speech.
Mr. Speaker, my time is rapidly running out, but I should now like to refer to the subject of business planning. Looking at the budget from a businessman's point of view is completely different from the point of view of the Government policy maker. The policy maker tends to look at long-term projects, whereas the business planner tends to plan ahead for two or three years. This budget lacks any pronouncement on longterm policies to give guidance to either businessmen or Government policy makers. It lacks short-term policies that would help the businessman plan his programs.
In view of the fact the Minister is tied to his own thinking, as indicated in the Royal Commission report of 1957, his remarks at the Kingston Conference of 1960, his book "Troubled Canada", published in 1960, and the budget of 1963, perhaps it would be propitious for me again to offer a few suggestions. I make these suggestions for the purpose of helping business planners know which way the Government wants them to go. I accept the premise that the expansion we all want will be accomplished primarily by private business, and I work on the assumption that the Government should set the climate and provide the objectives. These suggestions aim to achieve just that.
First, we need a sharp increase in the ceiling to which the 20 per cent income tax rate
April 29. 1965

for corporations applies, to a new level of approximately $100,000, in order to encourage expansion of family firms. If over-all corporate tax rates could be reduced, so much the better.
Second, we need excess write-offs of expenses incurred in promoting export sales in new markets for a three to four year period, or even longer.
Third, we need special tax treatment for export associations, even to the creation of a special legal entity for such associations. You will remember, Mr. Speaker, that we amended the Combines Investigation Act in 1959 to allow companies to combine for several purposes, one of which was related to exports. Now give them special tax treatment.
Fourth, we need special tax treatment for firms producing products which are subject to reduction in tariffs, once again for a three to five, or even ten-year adjustment period.
Fifth, we need a special liaison export committee, or an organization made up of the Departments of Trade and Commerce, Labour, Industry and Finance to operate on a continuing basis, with a permanent organization. This committee should be concerned with at least 14 different subjects, and I could list a dozen or more if I had the time. This liaison export committee, or organization, of these Departments should be concerned with the following: (1) assisting Canadian firms to get into the export business; (2) evaluating areas of specialization for Canadian business and recommending taxation incentives; (3) active encouragement for the formation of export associations where manufacturers are numerous and small; (4) promotion of training for Canadian business people in respect of export markets, such as travelling seminars; (5) coordination of all Canadian Government production and export activity with the plans of the Economic Council, and this would leave the Council politically free, but not unheeded, as it now seems to be; (6) a widening of the provisions of anti-combine and other legislation which tends to prevent mergers for exports; (7) improvement in trade where state controlled boards are concerned; (8) an increase in Canadian productivity-and there is still need for improvement in this field-; (9) the promotion of co-operation between Government and Canadian Export Associations; (10) the creation of new and improved export financing facilities; (11) the development of proposals for North American free trade in various products, when comparative advantage gives us a chance for accelerated

The Budget-Mr. Hamilton growth; (12) the development oi proposals for market development in respect of Canadian goods in underdeveloped areas, particularly related to foreign aid programs; (13) a reduction in the duplication of Federal and Provincial efforts in respect of trade promotion, and the co-ordination of all Canadian effort; and, finally, (14) we need promotion in respect of research of production and selling methods, and the dissemination of information.
Mr. Speaker, the House has been very cooperative in listening to me while listing these proposals. I made similar proposals last October and I hope that the Government will consider them. I have no wish just to criticize the Minister of Finance because he has not done everything that everyone desires, but I do think in respect of this matter of trade we should begin to bring forcibly to his attention the fact that Canada must, of necessity, concentrate on trade, regardless of how fast we expand our domestic markets, because we cannot keep up with potential primary and secondary production. We must find markets in the U.S.A. and in Europe, even though they produce the same products. We must move in a horizontal direction and get into these new markets where there is a great demand for our products. We must not only stick together politically on the North American continent, but in an economic way.
I do not know how I can create a word picture which everyone will understand, and I am sure that no one could do so, but let me suggest that sometimes I think we are much like Siamese twins: We cannot cut the knot which links us. But that does not mean we must lose our individualities. We must learn to walk and shift together, while preserving our own identities.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. My question of privilege relates to the order of speakers in this debate on the budget. I understand Your Honour has a list from which you are working today. I must say to you that the list you have is one that has not been agreed to by all the whips representing the various parties in the House. I must therefore protest against a change which is being made in the order of speakers.
Earlier this session in the debate on the
address, and likewise last session in the debate on the address and the debate on the budget, the agreement was, after we got through the first round of speakers, that there would be a block of nine speakers, three from the Liberal Party, three from the Progressive Conservative Party, and one each from the New Democratic Party, the Social Credit Party and the Ralliement Credi-tistes. Whether or not that pattern was satisfactory, it is the one that was agreed to and under which we have been operating.
Today, Mr. Speaker, an attempt has been made to change that pattern without the agreement of those concerned and, indeed, without consultation. I feel Your Honour should be advised that the list you have was not agreed to by three of the whips in this House, and until there is consultation and agreement to change the pattern we have had I believe you should continue recognizing Members in accordance with the pattern we have followed in the previous debates. I put this to you as a point of privilege for Your Honour's decision. If necessary, of course, I could move the appropriate motion, but it seems to me that in all fairness the plan we have been working under should not be changed without appropriate consultation.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
On the question of privilege, Mr. Speaker, to begin with I do not think it is a question of privilege because, as I understand the situation, it is the duty of the Speaker to see whatever Member he wishes to hear, and the only point raised by the hon. Member for Winnipeg North Centre was that you should not see the Member you had recognized. So it is not a matter of privilege. It is something that falls clearly within Your Honour's responsibility and jurisdiction.
As to the subject matter that the hon. Member raised, may I say I am not aware, except from his repeated assertions, that there is any such agreement, and if there is any such

agreement it seems to me it is manifestly unfair. I point out that the group he represents has 18 Members and if he will do a little arithmetic he will find that, if all Members are to be granted an equal hearing, a Member of his party would have the opportunity to speak every fifteenth speech.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is not mathematically correct.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Well, every fourteenth
speech. All I say in that regard is that all one has to do is divide 18 into 264, so I will let hon. Members do the arithmetic and make up their own minds whether or not what he suggests is fair. In any event, my arithmetic indicates to me that that would be the result.
So far in this debate we have had two Government speakers, two speakers from the Official Opposition and one from each of the other three groups. Now the hon. Member is asking that his group be given a second speaker, with the result that in two days of debate his group would have exactly the same debating right as the Government from the point of view of number of speakers. I do not know how far I need to develop the argument. The hon. Member's request seems to me to be patently unfair.
With regard to the point the hon. Member made about moving a motion, if he decides to put a motion we will have to vote on it and deal with it as I would hope it would be dealt with. With regard to his other proposition about consultation, may I say I will not be here tomorrow but if he feels some other arrangement should be made with regard to speaking I will be glad to call a meeting of the House Leaders on Monday morning.

port, just a matter of minutes ago if he had made any such commitment or agreement or arrangement, or what have you, when he was House Leader and my understanding is that he did not.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think the House should welcome this new breakthrough and should welcome the fait accompli on the part of the Government. We have had so few. It seems to me that the hon. Member for Winnipeg North Centre is the great guardian of the rules and customs of the House if it happens to suit his convenience. The order of speakers today and the ratio suggested by the Government House Leader reflects what the people of Canada, for good or bad, have done to Parliament, and I presume this can be changed at the next election.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Whistle all you like, my friend, but don't whistle here: I am not a mathematician but I have taken the trouble to calculate, and for the second time in this short speech may I say that the ratio suggested by the Government is fair. If we consider ratios as between the New Democratic Party, if I am allowed to name parties in the House, and the Government, the Govern-men has given up a speaker to whatever is to the left of the New Democratic Party, from the point of view of seating, but to the far right in every other way. I think we should press on with this fait accompli. I for one welcome it.
Mr. Pa+lerson: Mr. Speaker, it would seem to me that the hon. Member for Winnipeg North Centre has raised a legitimate question of privilege. The President of the Privy Council states that he does not have any knowledge of any understanding regarding the particular formula that has been in operation. I think he has been around here long enough to know just what has been going on. I do not think he has been keeping his eyes closed altogether. We have been working under this particular formula for some time now. At this moment we are not going to raise the question of whether or not the particular formula we have had is fair. In fact, personally I would go to the extent of saying it may not be fair. into his confidence and discuss the matter and perhaps we can arrive at a satisfactory formula. subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
On the question of privilege, Mr. Speaker.
The order of speakers is established by the various party whips or by the Speaker himself. If the whips are entrusted with that task, nothing has been done in that connection in this case; there has been no agreement between the whips. Consequently, if the order of speakers is to be determined by the whips, no change can be made tonight, in my opinion, since the whips have taken no decision in that respect.
If the question is settled by the Chair, then you are the one who must attend to it, Mr. Speaker. In the past, you set a precedent which was respected long enough to be recognized now. For the past two sessions, the order of speakers has always been the same in the house, during the debate on the Address in reply to the speech from the throne, during the budget debate or during discussion on a motion or resolution. Out of nine speakers, there were three Liberals, one Conservative, one member of the New Democratic party, one Thompsonnist and one member of the Ralliement Creditiste. If the decision is for the Speaker to take, then we are surprised to see you go against the precedent you have been following for years and take another attitude now.
What must we conclude from all that?
We note that the Conservatives and the Liberals get along like brothers, in this case, to try and diminish the contribution of the third parties to the work of the House of Commons. This constitutes an abnormal breach of the right of speech and of democracy.
On the other hand, Mr. Speaker, ever since I began to sit in this house, I always thought that the most important job of the Speaker was to protect the rights of the opposition. Now, the third parties in this house are the opposition. Even if we are a minority, even if the Liberal and the Conservative parties get together, the role of the Speaker is still one of protecting the opposition, including minority splinter parties.

April 29, 1965
Question of Privilege
The Liberal and Conservative parties may well vote with the majority, but I refuse to accept that the majority as such is always right. Majority does not necessarily mean righteousness and equity.
I think splinter parties, particularly under such circumstances, have to rely on the protection of the Speaker so that their right of speech may be fully recognized as it has always been in the past.
Let me say in conclusion that I am surprised by the stand taken by the leader of the government on this occasion. He is always asking for our co-operation, he is always seeking the co-operation of the opposition parties, yet today, when we have to settle a matter such as this, he starts by placing the matter before the house and then states that he will call a meeting of the house leaders. This is no way of co-operating. On the contrary, this is bound to indispose members of the opposition and it seems that the government house leader is now quite wrong and not playing the part he should as house leader, that is to organize peacefully the business of the house. He seems to be trying to provoke the opposition rather than obtain the co-operation of everybody. If the government house leader is trying to deprive us of our right of speech, I can assure him that we will find more occasions than he thinks to exercise that right in this house.
Mr. Speaker, the government house leader is suggesting that a meeting be held next Monday. We are willing to accept this proposal, but on condition that, until then, we follow the same order of speakers as in the past. Until then, we cannot accept that the order of speakers be changed and the meeting held afterwards.
If the government house leader is sincere, he will accept that, until next Monday, when the house leaders will meet again, we continue to follow the order previously established. That meeting will provide an opportunity for discussion. But there is no reason at all for making any change before the meeting takes place, because that would be acting in bad faith and a violation of the parliamentary and democratic rights of members of the smaller parties, who were elected to this house with a heavy percentage of the popular vote.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Tuesday of this week, as recorded at page 633 of Hansard, certain questions were put to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) regarding the transfer to Montreal of personnel employed at the Air Canada base at Winnipeg. The initial question on Tuesday was asked by the hon. Member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill), who wanted to know whether such transfers could not be postponed until the Thompson inquiry had been completed and the Government had announced its policy concerning the base. The Minister of Transport, if I may capsulize his reply, indicated that it was not the policy of the Government to intervene directly in the internal affairs of Air Canada. I then asked the Minister of Transport if he did not feel that the commitment given by the Government in the early part of 1964, one in which, as I understood it, Air Canada had concurred, should be honoured, and that during the lifetime of that commitment there should be no such transfers.
At that point there took place a brief altercation between the Minister of Transport and myself as to what the facts were, and it seemed to me that the proper resolution of that altercation was to post this question for a brief discussion in the overtime period.
[DOT] (10:10 p.m.)
I want to put to the Minister tonight a question in somewhat narrow terms. We are not at this point arguing the question whether or not the base should be transferred. The reason we are not arguing that at this point is because that whole question is in the hands of the Thompson inquiry. What we are concerned about is the matter of personnel being transferred from Winnipeg to Montreal prior to the completion of the Thompson inquiry

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion and the presentation of the report on the basis of that inquiry.
It is the contention of those of us from Winnipeg who have been following this matter, Mr. Speaker, that the commitment made by the Government in the House of Commons on November 22, 1963, should be honoured fully. On that day the Prime Minister indicated that the previously proposed phasing out of the Winnipeg base would not be proceeded with, but that the base would be maintained at full strength for a 10 year period. I asked in particular for a commitment that the number of employees at Winnipeg would be maintained. The answer of the then Minister of Transport, now the President of the Privy Council, was that that level would not only be maintained but might be increased.
Subsequently, Mr. Speaker, there was an exchange of telegrams, a rather warm exchange, between the Premier of Manitoba and the Prime Minister of Canada. Premier Rob-lin's telegram was dated February 13, 1964, and the Prime Minister's reply was dated February 14, 1964. In that telegram by the Prime Minister-I do not think it necessary that I read it-the Prime Minister confirmed that the position stated by the Government on November 22 still stood. He made it clear that there had not been a directive as such to what was then known as Trans-Canada Air Lines, but that there had been a statement of Government policy in which T.C.A., as it was then known, had concurred.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that these two statements in particular-the statement of the Prime Minister to the House of Commons on November 22, 1963, and the statement of the Prime Minister in his telegram to Premier Roblin on February 14, 1964-constituted a Government commitment that the base would stay there for 10 years and there would be no whittling away or diminution of the jobs at the Winnipeg base.
In the meantime, Mr. Speaker, quite a few personnel have been moved. I do not think we would argue over the number; it was of the order of 90. The Government contends on behalf of Air Canada that this has been done under the terms of a collective agreement. The point I wish to make, which is crucial to this whole situation, is that if these transfers are being made under what is referred to as an agreement, it is an agreement signed on or about March 13, 1964, practically a month after the Prime Minister's confirmation to Premier Roblin and several months after the commitment given to this House.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in view of the fact I have only three minutes in which to reply, I do not intend to apologize for reading one document.
The hon. gentleman pointed out that the collective agreement under which the company and the union are operating was concluded on March 13, 1964. The definitive

undertaking given to the Government of Manitoba was given in reply to a series of questions put to the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) by the Premier of Manitoba. If I remember correctly, these questions were posed both in this House and in the Manitoba legislature. I should like to read the first question asked, and the answer which was sent in the form of a telegram on March 21, 1964. The question is:
In terms of your statements in Parliament, what undertakings do you consider you have given about the maintenance of employment at the Winnipeg TCA overhaul base?
This is the Prime Minister's answer:
I said in Parliament on December 17 last year: "It is the policy of the government to do everything possible to maintain employment at the TCA base in Winnipeg and, if possible, to increase it."
So far as TCA is concerned, this means that the base will continue to be used for the overhaul of Viscount aircraft as long as these aircraft are in service.
As far as the government is concerned, it means further that we will do everything we can to ensure that other aircraft work is available in Winnipeg so that the eventual withdrawal of the Viscounts is at least balanced by new activities.
This policy should not be interpreted as a guarantee that each particular job now filled in Winnipeg will continue indefinitely. Normal changes in technology and work methods, and the provisions of seniority rules between employer and employee, may lead to the disappearance or transfer of particular jobs. A dynamic industry cannot be frozen into a particular employment pattern.
My undertakings mean that there will be no transfer of work from Winnipeg by deliberate policy. On the contrary, the policy is to do our utmost to secure enough aircraft work to maintain or improve the present employment level.
I have checked with Air Canada on each occasion of a transfer and I have been assured that every transfer from this base has been as a result of collective agreement and the operation of the seniority rule. I have not conducted a first-hand investigation into this matter, but I am sure that management has given me this assurance in good faith.

DEFENCE PRODUCTION-CENTRAL AGENCY FOR PURCHASE OF GOVERNMENT AUTOMOBILES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question involves the Minister of Industry (Mr. Drury) who is not in the House, but I am assured that the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Sharp) is going to speak on his behalf.
Since the first of the year there have been a number of rumours circulating that the Government of the day intends to institute a system of central purchasing of all nonmilitary cars and trucks for the Dominion Government. On April 6 the following question was placed on the Order Paper by the hon. Member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dins-dale):
1.	Has there been any recent departure from the policy of purchasing cars for the R.C.M.P. and the Department of Northern Affairs by having individual tenders from local dealers processed through the manufacturers concerned?
2.	If so, what is the nature of the change and for what reason was it made?
On Tuesday I asked the Minister of Industry if it was the intention of the Government to set up a central purchasing system and he advised me that it was the intention of the Government to do so. Several other hon. Members asked questions, all of which he was unable to answer at the time. Therefore I suggested I should like to bring up the matter for debate at ten o'clock at the first opportunity.
There are one or two questions I should like to ask the Minister and they are these. How does the Government propose to handle the resale of these cars? It should be noted that in most cases the Government purchases cars and trucks free of sales tax. If the Government then elected to place used vehicles on the market in direct competition with franchised dealers they would do so with a distinct advantage, and the disposal of a quantity of such vehicles in any given market area would have a serious effect on the automobile dealers in that area who are maintaining facilities for merchandising used vehicles.
Second, how does the Government propose to handle the servicing of these cars and trucks? The sale of a new vehicle usually entails such services being performed by the manufacturer's dealer representative in the area in which the new vehicle is delivered. Direct sale by the manufacturer, with direct delivery, suggests bypassing the dealer completely and raises the question of purchase

Third, how would the Government propose to handle the case where a Federal employee might wish to purchase a car through this proposed central purchasing system? There is another question of which I have not had a chance to give notice. How many cars and trucks would the Federal Government buy in one year?
I have no particular quarrel with the principle of central purchasing by the Government, but on behalf of the Automobile Dealers Association I must protest most vigorously any plan which will either put the Government in business in opposition to retail merchandisers or tend to destroy the service and the value of the franchise system. The franchised auto dealers constitute a large and respected industry. There are almost 5,000 of them in Canada. They employ about 72,000 people with a payroll of approximately $331 million a year, and yearly sales of almost $4 billion. So they do represent a large taxpaying group of people who are trying to provide a genuine, honest service to the people of Canada.
The franchise system has been built up over the years as the best method of automobile merchandising for the public, for the manufacturer and for the dealer. So I cannot think for a minute that it is the intention of the Government to help to destroy this industry, or to do anything that would be detrimental to this respected industry, which is providing a legitimate service. I ask the Minister, therefore, if he would answer those four questions which I have put to him?
